title: food as practice
hook: halfway through a good plate, the body says enough; Charaka and the Gita both have a word for that moment

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice began with Bhrigu, who searched for Brahman and first found food, and the vow: do not speak ill of food. Did a meal disappoint you, and did you let it go? Day one thousand three hundred eight.

Halfway through a plate of something really good, there's a moment. The food still tastes wonderful. Nothing has gone wrong. But somewhere under the pleasure, the body has quietly said: that's about right. It's a small signal, easy to sail straight past, especially with a few bites left and nobody watching. The old texts noticed that moment and gave it a word. The Charaka Samhita opens its chapter on the daily round with it, and the Bhagavad Gita makes it a condition for yoga. Today, the measure.
screen: `HALFWAY THROUGH A GOOD PLATE.` → `THE BODY SAYS: ABOUT RIGHT.` → `TODAY, THE MEASURE.`

segments.voice: The word is matra, measure. The chapter of Charaka that sets out the daily round begins, paraphrased: one should eat in measure. And then the important part. The measure isn't a fixed number for everyone. It depends on the strength of a person's digestive fire. The right amount is the amount that's digested well and in good time, without trouble. Your measure is yours. Elsewhere Charaka gives a picture that's easy to remember. Divide the stomach's room into three parts, it says. One part for solid food. One part for drink. And one part left for the body's own movements, the doshas, to work in. Paraphrased, but the picture really is that simple: don't fill it to the top. The Bhagavad Gita comes at the same moment from the side of practice. Krishna says, paraphrased, that yoga is not for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all. It's for the one who is measured in eating, and in sleeping and waking, in work and rest. For that person, he says, yoga becomes the end of sorrow. Put the two texts together. First, both texts reject the extremes. Not stuffing, and not starving. Second, measure isn't a rule handed down from outside. It's a listening, a matter of knowing your own fire. Third, it's a practice you get to try several times a day, at every meal, so it is never far away. The moment halfway through the plate is the whole lesson. The skill is hearing it.
screen: `MATRA: EAT IN MEASURE` · `THE MEASURE FOLLOWS YOUR FIRE` · `ONE PART LEFT EMPTY` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check in with the belly, without changing anything. Sit, and let the breath settle. Rest a hand on your stomach if you like. Ask, quietly: empty, part-full, or full? Don't answer with a judgment, just with what's there. Notice the breath moving under the hand. Notice whether there's room. Then let the question go and simply sit. If you pray, you can offer the next meal before it comes. The bell holds the time.
Food as practice. Matra, measure: the amount your own fire digests well, with room left over, neither too much nor too little. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. At your next meal, stop once halfway, put the fork or the bread down for three breaths, and ask whether you're still hungry. Day one thousand three hundred eight.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda eat in measure, the amount their digestion handles well, and leave some room in the stomach rather than eating until full, as the classical texts advise.

fork.setup: the plate is half gone, it still tastes great, and the body has quietly said: about right. what do the texts point you toward?
options: stop, or slow, and listen to the measure.
skip the next meal to make up for it.
fork.reveal: Charaka says to eat in measure, set by your own digestive fire, and the Gita rejects both overeating and not eating at all.

original.note: Sanskrit: matra, measure. Charaka's daily round begins with eating in measure.

trapdoor: what you thought: eating well means a strict portion size.
what it means: matra, measure, is the amount your own fire digests well, with room left over.

sources.ref: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 5 (one should eat in measure; the measure depends on the strength of the digestive fire)
Charaka Samhita, Vimanasthana 2 (the stomach in three parts: solid food, liquids, and space for the doshas)
Bhagavad Gita 6.16–17 (yoga is not for one who eats too much or not at all; for one measured in food, recreation, work, sleep and waking, yoga destroys sorrow)

notes: Charaka Sutrasthana 5.3 (matrashi syat) and the measure depending on agni bala: confirm. Day 1293 also mentions this chapter opening with measure in food; this day develops it.

Charaka Vimanasthana 2.3: confirm the three-part division of the stomach (one for solids, one for liquids, one for vata, pitta, kapha), paraphrased here as 'left empty, so the body's own movements have room to work'.
Gita 6.16–17: confirm paraphrase, including 'and in sleeping and waking, in work and rest' and 'yoga becomes the end of sorrow'.
Day 1293 (dinacharya) already noted that Sutrasthana 5 opens with measure; this day is the fuller treatment.

Editor: Vimanasthana 2 leaves the third part for the doshas, not 'empty'; teach, word, match and myth now say so. Replaced the 'Think of' phrasing; changed the practice's closing line so it doesn't repeat 1302's thanks for a last meal; varied the transition.
